"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: The question removes the closed-loop dependency: it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes.
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers)
Steering a VLA's internal features can bring out behaviour the model already has, without retraining. On real DROID hardware, SAE steering of pi0.5 raised target-object grasps by +9 to +21 out of 25 trials, and ablating the top-4 general features cut success from 39/40 to 0/40. COAST conceptors raised pi0.5 on LIBERO-10 from 0.43 to 0.80, with about +40% on three real tasks. Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot on a UR10e). All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or a dish rack. Goodfire markets steering for robotics but publishes no numbers.
What more compute would buy: The quantity is closed-loop rollouts and SAEs swept; the largest is 420,000+ rollouts and 520+ SAEs across six VLAs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233), and above that it is unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
What runs step after step: Each feature waits on an SAE fit (about 6,700 Adam steps, derived from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19183; 'a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100') and then on closed-loop rollouts of up to 300 steps, each waiting on a ~150 ms VLA forward pass and the next observation; the answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features (20,250 episodes), and one unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps. Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments in a GPU-parallel simulator, with a separate hook per environment and simulation pipelined against inference, would run them together; this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth). The nearest attempt is RLinf-VLA, 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments, for RL rather than interpretability (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06710v2).
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"The answer needed 150 rollouts x 135 features = 20,250 closed-loop episodes, each up to 300 sequential steps at ~150 ms per VLA forward pass, with the GPU idle while the simulator steps; every feature pays this full episode cost regardless of effect size.\",\"assumption\":\"A feature's value can only be measured by closed-loop task success, so every candidate feature must be paid for in full episodes before anything is known about it.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the measured quantity from closed-loop success to open-loop steered action divergence: record a fixed batch of states from the target domain (including cloth-folding and dish-rack demonstrations), and measure how much each steering direction changes the policy's predicted action chunk in one batched forward pass. This turns per-feature evaluation from a sequential 300-step episode into an embarrassingly parallel (state, steering) forward-pass job; closed-loop rollouts are then spent only on the top-k features by divergence.\",\"question\":\"Does the ranking of features by open-loop steered action-chunk divergence on recorded states match the ranking by closed-loop success-rate delta, measured as Spearman rho over ~30 features on 3 tasks?\",\"measure\":\"Reuse one existing pi0.5 SAE; compute L2 divergence of predicted action chunks for 30 steering directions over ~10k replay states (~2-5 GPU-hours on one A100), and get ground truth from 30 features x 50 rollouts = 1,500 episodes batched in a GPU simulator (~15-25 GPU-hours). Total roughly 1-2 GPU-days.\",\"compute_after\":\"If rho is high, screening 520+ SAEs and thousands of features becomes a pure forward-pass workload that splits perfectly across GPUs, and rollout budget concentrates on a handful of features; more compute buys feature coverage instead of repeated episodes.\",\"exact\":\"Spearman rho (with bootstrap CI) between the open-loop action-chunk divergence ranking and the closed-loop success-delta ranking across 30 features x 3 tasks.\",\"expected\":\"rho around 0.5-0.8: ablating just the top-4 general features already collapses success from 39/40 to 0/40, so large steering effects should be directly visible in action space.\",\"fails_if\":\"Steering effects are dominated by closed-loop contact feedback (compounding errors that only appear at step 200+), so open-loop divergence on replay states is uncorrelated with success; this failure is most likely exactly for cloth and dish-rack contact, the cases that matter.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Standard SAE feature-effect dashboards that measure activation-to-output effects without rollouts (Goodfire/Anthropic-style), and Grant et al.'s replay-based probe that found motor programs bound to absolute UR10e coordinates.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"A fixed 150 rollouts per feature spends most of the 20,250 episodes confirming null effects, and binary success at step 300 is the highest-variance measurable quantity, which forces the large n in the first place.\",\"assumption\":\"Every feature must receive an equal, pre-committed rollout budget, and the objective is to estimate each feature's success rate rather than to find the few features that matter.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the objective from per-feature rate estimation to best-arm identification: successive-rejects or UCB allocation that early-eliminates features whose effect is statistically bounded near zero, and replace the binary yes/no outcome with a per-step progress score (distance-to-goal or grasp quality), which has lower variance per rollout and shrinks the n needed for each comparison.\",\"question\":\"How many episodes does successive-rejects allocation need to recover the same top-5 features as the fixed 150x135 sweep with probability at least 0.95, and what episode savings factor does the per-step progress score add?\",\"measure\":\"Answer offline: replay the existing 20,250-episode sweep outcomes (or run one 20k-episode sim sweep at RLinf-VLA-style throughput, tens of GPU-hours with 256 parallel envs) and simulate the bandit allocation and both outcome metrics on the recorded data; CPU-hours if logs exist, otherwise tens of GPU-hours once.\",\"compute_after\":\"Rollout compute concentrates on the informative tail instead of uniform confidence intervals on zeros; more compute then buys 10x deeper feature libraries rather than tighter estimates of features that do nothing.\",\"exact\":\"Episodes-to-top-5 at P(correct) >= 0.95 under successive rejects versus fixed allocation on recorded sweep data, plus the variance ratio of binary success versus per-step progress score.\",\"expected\":\"A 3-10x episode reduction, because the effect distribution appears bimodal (top-4 ablation alone kills behaviour; most features do nothing), which is exactly the regime where best-arm identification wins most.\",\"fails_if\":\"Steering effects are many, small, and uniform (+1-2% across dozens of features), so no arm can be eliminated early and adaptive allocation saves little over the fixed budget.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Successive-rejects and UCB best-arm identification (Audibert, Bubeck, Munos 2010); adaptive-subsampling LLM evaluation; RLinf-VLA's 256-environment 1.61-1.88x throughput as the batched-rollout substrate.\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"Above 420,000 rollouts and 520 SAEs it is still unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks; and where sim steering does not match the real robot (stated false for cloth), each additional simulated rollout buys a tighter estimate of a quantity that does not transfer, i.e., more of the same.\",\"assumption\":\"The path to cloth and dish-rack steering is to scale simulation sweeps, meaning feature effects found in simulation are assumed to transfer to real hardware.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the measured quantity from success rate in sim to the transfer coefficient itself: for a small set of features, estimate each one's steering effect (success-rate delta) in both a deformable-object simulator and on real hardware, and measure the cross-domain rank correlation. This is a small, decisive experiment that gates whether any large deformable sim sweep should be run at all.\",\"question\":\"What is the Spearman correlation between per-feature steering effects measured in a deformable simulator and on the real robot, over ~10 features on one cloth task (towel fold) and one dish-rack task?\",\"measure\":\"10 features x 30 episodes x 2 tasks x 2 domains: 600 batched sim episodes (a few GPU-hours with parallel environments) and 600 real episodes at ~3-5 minutes each with resets, about 40-50 robot-hours, i.e., roughly 1-2 weeks on one DROID-class arm and a few thousand dollars of operator time; real-robot time dominates.\",\"compute_after\":\"If rho is high, sim compute becomes worth scaling to thousands of features on deformable tasks; if rho is near 0, compute redirects to real-world rollouts with bandit allocation or real replay-state screening, and no large GPU sim sweep on cloth is run.\",\"exact\":\"Spearman rho (with bootstrap CI) between sim and real per-feature success deltas across 10 features x 2 tasks, reported per task.\",\"expected\":\"rho moderate-to-high for the rigid dish-rack components (consistent with the +9 to +21 real gains from sim-screened SAE steering on DROID hardware) and unknown, possibly near 0, for cloth.\",\"fails_if\":\"At 30 real episodes per feature the binomial standard error (~0.09) exceeds the true effect sizes, so the correlation estimate is noise-dominated; the measurement must then switch to a continuous per-step progress score or more episodes before any conclusion.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Sim2Real predictivity studies measuring sim-vs-real policy-rank correlation (Kadian et al., SIMPAR 2019); the problem statement's own note that steering effects in sim do not match real for cloth; RLinf-VLA as the batched-sim substrate.\"}]
